newsitem.title: FRANCE: Santer gently rebukes French on EU foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Santer gently rebukes French on EU foreign policy.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer took a veiled swipe at France on Thursday for preaching a common European foreign policy while pursuing national diplomacy when it really mattered.

Without singling out Paris by name, Santer said in a speech to the French Institute for International Relations that some of the big European Union member states only turned to common action when it suited them, notably in the Middle East.
"Some of our big countries still perceive European foreign policy as one option among others, which should be used or left aside according to circumstances," he said in remarks prepared for delivery.

"Europe is easily forgotten when it comes to reviving the Middle East peace process," Santer said in a dig both at Paris and at the United States, which excluded the EU -- the biggest paymaster of the peace process -- from last week's summit.
France sent its foreign minister to mediate between Israel and Lebanese Hizbollah guerrillas in April and informed its EU partners as an afterthought.
President Jacques Chirac cited historic ties to the region to seek a bigger role for France in Middle East peacemaking.

Santer said there were two drawbacks to such a selective use of an EU foreign policy: instruments used only intermittently could not be relied upon to work in serious crises, and the EU had more means of exerting influence in common via trade, aid and finance than member states had individually.
"We must draw the consequences of this already very far advanced movement towards European unification," he said.

Santer said Europe's influence in the Balkans, Russia and the Middle East did not properly reflect its financial contribution, and it was up to the Europeans to act in way that turned their weight into force.

"From what I hear and read, I note that two phenomena are particularly irritating: on the one hand, the absence of action, and on the other, the autonomous actions of some member states," the commission chief said.

"The second infant malady of European foreign policy is this temptation of some of our member states to act as trailblazers, or simply to act alone...mostly not out of a lack of European conviction but simply because these states only have a choice between a policy of worthy intentions and national action," he said.

"Even when we are united, as is largely the case on the Middle East, it is extremely difficult to change the image of disunion which conventional wisdom gives of us. That leads to situations such as the recent case when (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu thanked the EU for not taking a more active part in reviving the peace process," Santer added.

The Eu needed to improve its policy planning and decision making system, make more use of majority voting in applying agreed foreign policy and develop a real capacity for taking European military decisions, he said.
